name: Fewest tokens, largest first
brief:
An arcade sells tokens of the different values in `values`, with as many of each as needed. A prize costs `amount` exactly. Return the tokens of a payment that uses the fewest tokens, listed from largest to smallest. When several fewest payments exist, return the one that comes first when the lists are compared from the front, largest value first. Return `[]` when `amount` cannot be paid.

Write `fewest_tokens(values, amount)`.

Example. For `values = [1, 4, 5, 6]` and `amount = 15`, three tokens are needed. Both `[6, 5, 4]` and `[5, 5, 5]` use three, and `[6, 5, 4]` starts with the larger token. The answer is `[6, 5, 4]`.
constraints: $1 \le$ `amount` $\le 20{,}000$. `values` holds 1 to 15 different token values from 1 to 10,000.
$O(\text{amount} \times k)$ time is the target for $k$ values. Plain recursion without a memo is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Fill `need[a]`, the fewest tokens for each amount up to `amount`. Then rebuild the payment from the top: at each step take the largest value `v` with `need[a - v] == need[a] - 1`.

examples.note: Two tokens make at most 12, so three is the fewest; `[6, 5, 4]` beats `[5, 5, 5]` at the first place.
No mix of 4s and 9s makes 14, so the prize cannot be paid.

how: Submit runs 15 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method is plain recursion that tries each token first and solves the rest again, which repeats the same amounts and runs out of time from about 60 upwards. The step to the target is the table `need`, filled once from 1 to `amount`, which also lets the payment be rebuilt without searching. Unlike the usual task, which asks only for the count, the answer is the payment itself with a tie rule, so the table is read back from the top, largest token first.
notes: `need[a]` is one more than the best `need[a - v]`, because the last token of any payment is one of the values.
Rebuilding with the largest `v` that keeps `need[a - v] == need[a] - 1` gives the list that wins from the front, and it comes out largest first.
The table has `amount` entries, each checked against $k$ values, so the work is $O(\text{amount} \times k)$.

planted.slip: Taking the largest token while it fits is a greedy that can use more tokens, or miss a payment that exists.
Recording the smallest token that reaches each amount finds a fewest payment, but not always the one the tie rule asks for.
Plain recursion for the fewest tokens is right but tries every order of the same tokens, too slow.
Rebuilding the payment without checking `v <= a` reads `need[a - v]` at a negative index, the far end of the table.
Applying the tie rule to the first token only and following a stored token for the rest can return a payment that is not the largest first.
